items.readable_text:
Content:
In a previous lesson, we saw how big-O notation [MATH: O(g(n))] is used to construct a set containing all functions bounded above by [MATH: cg(n),] where [MATH: g(n)] is a nonnegative function, [MATH: c] is a positive constant and [MATH: n] is sufficiently large. This definition helps classify the behavior of algorithms as the parameter [MATH: n] increases.

Content:
If particular, if [MATH: f(n)\in O(g(n)),] then [MATH: cg(n)] is an asymptotic upper bound for [MATH: f(n)] as [MATH: n\to\infty.]

Content:
In this lesson, we'll discuss big-omega notation, which helps us to define asymptotic lower bounds for functions as [MATH: n\to\infty.]

Content:
The notation [MATH: \Omega(g(n))] defines the set of all functions [MATH: f(n)] for which there exist positive constants [MATH: c] and [MATH: n_0] such that for all [MATH: n] larger than [MATH: n_0,] the values of [MATH: f(n)] are not smaller than [MATH: c \cdot g(n){:}]

Content:
[MATH: \Omega(g(n)) = \big\{ f(n) \: : \: \exists c, n_0 > 0, \: \forall n \geq n_0, \: 0 \leq c g(n) \leq f(n) \big\}]

Content:
Geometrically, this means that starting from a certain point [MATH: n=n_0,] the graph [MATH: y=c \cdot g(n)] lies below the graph of [MATH: y=f(n)] for [MATH: n\geq n_0.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/343529817175eacda670a2ecb6423c64]

Content:
For example, the set [MATH: \Omega(n^2)] is defined as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \Omega(n^2) = \big\{ f(n) \: : \:
\exists c, n_0 > 0
, \:
\forall n \geq n_0
, \:
0 \leq c\cdot n^2 \leq f(n)\big\}]

Content:
Thus, the following statements are all true:

Content:
- [MATH: n^3 \in \Omega(n^2)] since [MATH: 0\leq 1\cdot n^2\leq n^3] for all [MATH: n\geq 1.]
- [MATH: n^3 \in \Omega(n^3)] since [MATH: 0\leq \dfrac12\cdot n^3\leq n^3] for all [MATH: n\geq 1.]
- [MATH: n^3 \in \Omega(1)] since [MATH: 0\leq 10\cdot 1 \leq n^3] for all [MATH: n\geq 3.]

Content:
However, [MATH: n^3\notin \Omega(n^4)] since there are no constants [MATH: c] and [MATH: n_0] such that [MATH: 0\leq c\cdot n^4 \leq n^3] for [MATH: n\geq n_0.] Intuitively, the function [MATH: cn^4] will always outgrow [MATH: n^3] eventually.

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
According to the definition, [MATH: \Omega(g(n))] is the set of all functions [MATH: f(n),] for which there exist positive constants [MATH: c] and [MATH: n_0] such that for all [MATH: n] larger than [MATH: n_0,] the values of [MATH: f(n)] are not smaller than [MATH: c g(n){:}] [MATH: \Omega(g(n)) = \big\{ f(n) \: : \: \exists c, n_0 > 0, \: \forall n \geq n_0, \: 0 \leq c g(n)\leq f(n) \big\}]

So, we start as shown below.

We need to show that there exists a constant [MATH: c] such that for sufficiently large [MATH: n,] we have [MATH: 8n^2-5 \geq c n.]

Now, let's isolate [MATH: c] on the right-hand side of the inequality.

Dividing both sides of the inequality by [MATH: n,] we get the follows: [MATH: 8n^{2} − 5|≥ cn; (8n^{2} − 5)/(n)|≥ (cn)/(n); (8n^{2})/(n) − (5)/(n)|≥ (cn)/(n); 8n − (5)/(n)|≥ c]

Notice that [MATH: 8n=8] and [MATH: \dfrac{5}{n}=5] if [MATH: n=1.] Also, [MATH: 8n] monotonically approaches [MATH: \infty] and [MATH: \dfrac{5}{n}] monotonically approaches [MATH: 0] as [MATH: n \to \infty.] As a result, [MATH: 8n-\dfrac{5}{n} \geq 3] for all [MATH: n \geq 1,] and we can now pick our constants.

By setting [MATH: n_0=1] and [MATH: c=3,] we make the above inequality hold for any [MATH: n \geq n_0.]

Of course, other choices for the constants [MATH: c] and [MATH: n_0] may do the job, but the important thing is we found at least one such combination.

Therefore, [MATH: 8n^2-5 \in \Omega(n).]

Content:
Earlier, we saw that

Content:
[MATH: n^3 \in \Omega(n^2), \qquad n^3 \in \Omega(n^3), \qquad n^3 \notin \Omega(n^4).]

Content:
In fact, for any function [MATH: f\in \Omega(n^3)] that's bounded below by [MATH: cn^3] for sufficiently large [MATH: n,] it must also be bounded below by a function of the form [MATH: kn^2,] where [MATH: k] is a constant. Therefore, it follows that [MATH: f\in \Omega(n^2),] and since this is true for any [MATH: f\in\Omega(n^3),] we have
[MATH: \Omega(n^2) \supset \Omega(n^3).]

Content:
By similar reasoning, it follows that
[MATH: \Omega(n^2) \supset \Omega(n^3) \supset \Omega(n^4).]

Content:
We can summarize the scales of certain frequently used functions in terms of big-Omega notation in the diagram below.

Graphic:

Content:
Here, we have the following inclusions:

Content:
[MATH: \Omega(1) \supset \Omega(\log(n)) \supset \Omega(n) \supset \Omega(n\log(n)) \supset \Omega(n^k) \supset \Omega(a^n) \supset \Omega(n!)]

Content:
Furthermore, [MATH: \Omega(n^k) \supset \Omega(n^{k+1})] for all [MATH: k=2,3,\ldots] and [MATH: \Omega(a^n) \supset \Omega(b^n)] whenever [MATH: a < b.] Notice that all inclusions are proper.

Content:
Also, we'll use the following two facts:

Content:
- If [MATH: c] is any constant,
[MATH: \Omega(c g(n)) = \Omega(g(n)).]
- If [MATH: \Omega(g(n)) \supset \Omega(f(n)),] then
[MATH: \Omega(g(n)+f(n)) = \Omega(f(n)).]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
In a previous lesson, we saw how big-O notation [MATH: O(g(n))] is used to construct a set containing all functions bounded above by [MATH: cg(n),] where [MATH: g(n)] is a nonnegative function, [MATH: c] is a positive constant and [MATH: n] is sufficiently large. This definition helps classify the behavior of algorithms as the parameter [MATH: n] increases.

Content:
If particular, if [MATH: f(n)\in O(g(n)),] then [MATH: cg(n)] is an asymptotic upper bound for [MATH: f(n)] as [MATH: n\to\infty.]

Content:
In this lesson, we'll discuss big-omega notation, which helps us to define asymptotic lower bounds for functions as [MATH: n\to\infty.]

Content:
The notation [MATH: \Omega(g(n))] defines the set of all functions [MATH: f(n)] for which there exist positive constants [MATH: c] and [MATH: n_0] such that for all [MATH: n] larger than [MATH: n_0,] the values of [MATH: f(n)] are not smaller than [MATH: c \cdot g(n){:}]

Content:
[MATH: \Omega(g(n)) = \big\{ f(n) \: : \: \exists c, n_0 > 0, \: \forall n \geq n_0, \: 0 \leq c g(n) \leq f(n) \big\}]

Content:
Geometrically, this means that starting from a certain point [MATH: n=n_0,] the graph [MATH: y=c \cdot g(n)] lies below the graph of [MATH: y=f(n)] for [MATH: n\geq n_0.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/343529817175eacda670a2ecb6423c64]

Content:
For example, the set [MATH: \Omega(n^2)] is defined as follows:

Content:
[MATH: \Omega(n^2) = \big\{ f(n) \: : \:
\exists c, n_0 > 0
, \:
\forall n \geq n_0
, \:
0 \leq c\cdot n^2 \leq f(n)\big\}]

Content:
Thus, the following statements are all true:

Content:
- [MATH: n^3 \in \Omega(n^2)] since [MATH: 0\leq 1\cdot n^2\leq n^3] for all [MATH: n\geq 1.]
- [MATH: n^3 \in \Omega(n^3)] since [MATH: 0\leq \dfrac12\cdot n^3\leq n^3] for all [MATH: n\geq 1.]
- [MATH: n^3 \in \Omega(1)] since [MATH: 0\leq 10\cdot 1 \leq n^3] for all [MATH: n\geq 3.]

Content:
However, [MATH: n^3\notin \Omega(n^4)] since there are no constants [MATH: c] and [MATH: n_0] such that [MATH: 0\leq c\cdot n^4 \leq n^3] for [MATH: n\geq n_0.] Intuitively, the function [MATH: cn^4] will always outgrow [MATH: n^3] eventually.

---

Explanation:
According to the definition, [MATH: \Omega(g(n))] is the set of all functions [MATH: f(n)] for which there exist positive constants [MATH: c] and [MATH: n_0] such that for all [MATH: n] larger than [MATH: n_0,] the values of [MATH: f(n)] are not smaller than [MATH: c \cdot g(n){:}]

[MATH: \Omega(g(n)) = \big\{ f(n) \: : \: \exists c, n_0 > 0, \: \forall n \geq n_0, \: 0 \leq c g(n) \leq f(n) \big\}]

Geometrically, this means the following:

> The set [MATH: \Omega(6^n)] consists of all functions [MATH: f(n)] for which there exist positive constants [MATH: c] and [MATH: n_0] such that the graph of [MATH: y=c \cdot 6^n] lies below the graph of [MATH: y=f(n)] for all [MATH: n\geq n_0.]

Item 5 — Example: Proving That a Function Belongs to a Big-Omega Set

Example Prompt:
Let [MATH: n \in \mathbb{N}.] Prove that [MATH: 8n^2-5 \in \Omega(n).]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
According to the definition, [MATH: \Omega(g(n))] is the set of all functions [MATH: f(n),] for which there exist positive constants [MATH: c] and [MATH: n_0] such that for all [MATH: n] larger than [MATH: n_0,] the values of [MATH: f(n)] are not smaller than [MATH: c g(n){:}]
[MATH: \Omega(g(n)) = \big\{ f(n) \: : \: \exists c, n_0 > 0, \: \forall n \geq n_0, \: 0 \leq c g(n)\leq f(n) \big\}]

So, we start as shown below.

> We need to show that there exists a constant [MATH: c] such that for sufficiently large [MATH: n,] we have
> [MATH: 8n^2-5 \geq c n.]

Now, let's isolate [MATH: c] on the right-hand side of the inequality.

> Dividing both sides of the inequality by [MATH: n,] we get the follows:
> [MATH: 8n^{2} − 5|≥ cn; (8n^{2} − 5)/(n)|≥ (cn)/(n); (8n^{2})/(n) − (5)/(n)|≥ (cn)/(n); 8n − (5)/(n)|≥ c]

Notice that [MATH: 8n=8] and [MATH: \dfrac{5}{n}=5] if [MATH: n=1.] Also, [MATH: 8n] monotonically approaches [MATH: \infty] and [MATH: \dfrac{5}{n}] monotonically approaches [MATH: 0] as [MATH: n \to \infty.] As a result,
[MATH: 8n-\dfrac{5}{n} \geq 3]
for all [MATH: n \geq 1,] and we can now pick our constants.

> By setting [MATH: n_0=1] and [MATH: c=3,] we make the above inequality hold for any [MATH: n \geq n_0.]

Of course, other choices for the constants [MATH: c] and [MATH: n_0] may do the job, but the important thing is we found at least one such combination.

> Therefore, [MATH: 8n^2-5 \in \Omega(n).]

The full proof is given below.

> We need to show that there exists a constant [MATH: c] such that for sufficiently large [MATH: n,] we have
> [MATH: 8n^2-5 \geq c n.]
> Dividing both sides of the inequality by [MATH: n,] we get the follows:
> [MATH: 8n^{2} − 5|≥ cn; (8n^{2} − 5)/(n)|≥ (cn)/(n); (8n^{2})/(n) − (5)/(n)|≥ (cn)/(n); 8n − (5)/(n)|≥ c]
> By setting [MATH: n_0=1] and [MATH: c=3,] we make the above inequality hold for any [MATH: n \geq n_0.]
>
> Therefore, [MATH: 8n^2-5 \in \Omega(n).]
